_about: Per-tab CCL manifests (voice_guide_redesign.md sections 3, 8, 9). Each tab declares its supported verbs (caps) and its knob dimensions with a DOM binding + spoken aliases. Consumed by BOTH the shell (explorer.html builds the active tab's ctx from this) and the coverage audit (every live interactive control on a tab must be a bound knob or an explicit exclusion -- unbound control => loud pre-push failure, section 9). Adding a T1 tab is ONE entry here plus a knowledge default file -- never a new tool, prompt, or session-schema change. Knob `values[].v` are the real DOM option values (NOT their display labels); `aka` are the spoken forms a user would say. A knob carries `aka` too, because the word PRINTED on a control is not always its id -- metabolism's `metric` select is labelled Amplitude on screen, so `label` must mirror the live UI text and `aka` must cover what a user would actually say. Knob names and aliases MUST be single tokens: the parser takes `set <knob> <value...>` and reads the knob as the first word, so a two-word alias is unparseable, not merely unmatched. Keys beginning with _ are documentation and ignored by consumers. GESTURES: each tab must also declare its non-DOM interaction surface (zoom, pan, drag, click, hover) -- the runtime sweep enumerates ELEMENTS and is structurally blind to gestures, so they are declared and the gate checks the declaration is honest: `covered` must name verbs the tab actually has in caps, `deferred` must name its increment, `excluded` must give a reason, and a tab declaring nothing FAILS (silence is not a completeness claim).

sociogram._knobs_note: Sociogram's affordances are filters/selection/highlight/camera (their own dim kinds, not `set` knobs). It carries no `set` verb in v1. Listed here so the shell can read one uniform per-tab source; its caps mirror the engine's SOCIOGRAM_CAPS until step 2 migrates the shell to read caps from this file.

knobs.label: Summa-in-1-year Transcript

It is drawn as two buttons, which knobs could not bind (a <select> or a checkbox only), and its winning class is `.on`, not the `.active` a view's test hard-codes. Declaring it as a view would have been mis-declaring it to fit the machinery; the `buttons` bind kind is the honest fix and is portable to every button-group toggle in the fan-out. Both sides are gated on the entry actually HAVING that file (switchMode returns early otherwise), and neither does anything until an article is open.

items._note:
ONE FLAT ROSTER OF VISIBLE ROWS at all three levels, not three level-scoped rosters. `when` can only ask which sub-view is active, and nothing on this page says which LEVEL a user is walking -- there is no such state to read, because a sighted user is not at a level either, they are looking at an open tree. So `next` walks exactly the visual reading order and `open` on a part or a question expands it, which makes the roster GROW as you go. That growth is reported, because expanding a container and loading an article are the same verb on the same tree and would otherwise sound identical.
NO `total` DECLARED, deliberately. #stats-line counts ARTICLES (2656 of 2747 available) while this roster counts ROWS; wiring it up would make `what` say '24 of 2747 entries', which is false in unit rather than merely imprecise. Speaking the availability line honestly is its own declaration -- curriculum tools increment 2.
`.a-row.avail` only: 91 articles have no transcript yet and carry NO click handler at all, so offering them would be offering a door that does not open.
items._reads_note: Where the page PUTS what a row opens -- the RENDERED MARKDOWN, not the pane around it. #content-area was the first guess and it wrapped the article in the page's own chrome: the reader opened with the ref, the title, the day, and then read the two mode buttons aloud ('Summa-in-1-year Transcript', 'Contemporary Synthesis?') before reaching a word of Aquinas. It also hid every per-block filter, because the whole article arrived as ONE child node whose textContent carried the provenance blockquotes and headings inside it. #md-body is the markdown itself, so its children are the blocks and the reader can tell prose from furniture. Without it `read` spoke the tree row -- 'A1 Article 1 Day 2', five words -- and called it the article.
items._read_variants_note: One article, two renderings. Asked for 'the commentary', a human guide turns to it and reads -- they do not explain that a toggle exists, and then wait to be asked again (Tom, 2026-07-27). A variant is NOT a new dimension: it writes the `mode` knob the tab already has, so `set mode synthesis` and `read the commentary` end in the same state. The read waits for the page's fetch, because reading straight after the click would speak the PREVIOUS rendering and announce it as the new one.
items._locate_note: An ADDRESS, which is none of the things `go` already resolves -- not a tab, not a sub-view, not a link. Summa's refs are I.Q4.A2 and only Summa knows that, so the scheme is declared and the shell only knows how to read `locate`. A level left unsaid is taken from where the user already is (the part of the question currently open) and the guess is SAID, because a wrong part is a plausible-sounding wrong answer rather than an obvious failure. `open_first` opens closed ancestors, since a target inside a collapsed container is addressable but not reachable -- marking it silently would be pointing at a shut door.
items._search_note: What a docent knows without knowing everything: not the Summa by heart, but roughly where things live, and how to look (Tom, 2026-07-27: 'take me to a question on angelic knowledge'). The tab already holds all 611 question titles in its own indexData at boot, so this is a plain title match -- deliberately NOT a model call or an embedding. Deterministic, free, testable, and it never bills the broker. QUESTIONS ONLY in this increment: article titles are mostly null in the index (the row renders 'Article N'), so searching them would return a list of indistinguishable numbers. Resolved LAST in the `go` chain, after tabs, views, coordinates, renderings and links, because it is the broadest net and must never shadow something named outright. One clear winner lands; anything else is named back, since silently choosing among four is indistinguishable from being right when there is no screen.

items._note: The Summa sociogram is the wiki_narration graph one document down, pre-cut to Summa nodes. Its nodes are walkable in principle -- revealedNodes() already knows this exact artifact -- but that reader is hard-wired to the tab's OWN document (ifWin/ifDoc) and does not take a frame the way domItems does. Generalising it is the prs_3d increment's job, not this one's, so the view is reachable and honest about being unwalkable rather than silently returning an empty roster.

prs_3d._caps_note: THE FIRST TAB WITH NO ELEMENTS TO WALK. Its 507 narratives are drawn into a WebGL canvas -- the whole tab is one <div id="canvas-container"> -- so there is nothing for domItems to enumerate and nothing for getClientRects to be asked about. The Sociogram looks like the same case and is not: d3 leaves an SVG circle per node behind, which is why revealedNodes could read `.node-circle` and pass for the general adapter. It never was one; it was the SVG case. So the roster here is read from the page's OWN data (`meshes`, the three.js scene objects) through declared dotted paths, and `open` is a declared CALL rather than a click -- see the items spec. NO `find` yet: the highlight dim reads a class stamp off SVG opacities and `search` ends in el.click(), both DOM-shaped. The CAMERA, by contrast, is now declared -- see `camera`. It was deferred for exactly one session on the grounds that execCamera was Sociogram-specific, and Tom's answer was the right one: a tab built around an orbiting camera that voice cannot turn is a room the guide can walk up to and never walk around.

knobs.label: Edges (threads)
knobs._note: The P-R-S threads within one narrative. A bool rather than a member of the Sociogram's `edges` FAMILY on purpose: that family is a `showEdgeType` map batch-written through refreshSimLinks, and this tab has three independent booleans and one applyPRSFilters. Inheriting the family binds would be the exact mistake the Community Explorer manifest was warned off (2026-07-26).

prs_3d._knobs_note: Three booleans, no `views`. NO SUB-VIEWS AT ALL here, which is worth saying out loud because the standing trap of this fan-out is a view whose name is also a tab: three of the first six collided (2026-07-26). This tab has one surface, so there is nothing to collide.

items._note:
ONE ITEM IS THREE MESHES. A PRS narrative is drawn as a problem, a resource and a solution sharing one triplet id, so without `dedupe` the guide would walk every narrative three times and report a count the page itself contradicts -- updatePrsCount dedupes by triplet id for exactly this reason, and `total` reads that same line so the two numbers cannot drift.
`visible` is the page's own three.js flag, which is what applyPRSFilters writes: it is the same question getClientRects answers in the DOM, asked where this page keeps the answer.
`activate` names prsSearchClickResult, which is what the page's OWN search results call -- so voice opens a narrative by the same road a click does, including the camera move onto it. That matters more here than anywhere: with 507 nodes in three dimensions, selecting something off-screen and saying nothing would be indistinguishable from doing nothing.
NO SORT, unlike the Sociogram's alphabetical roster. Source order is the order the page built them, grouped by tradition and then by date; the labels open "P1 (Text, referenced in ...)" so sorting them alphabetically would produce an order that means nothing to anyone.
items._selected_note: A window PATH, not a selector, because a canvas has nothing to carry a class. Same rule as Summa's `.a-row.sel` -- read the PAGE's marker rather than the click we just made -- and it is what closes the FIFTH which-document instance the 2026-07-27 handoff said to expect: `read` decides what to call the thing by asking whether the marked ELEMENT is still attached, which a canvas roster can never answer yes to, so the reader fell through to #right-page-title (absent here) and called a narrative "this article".
items._label_note: 222 OF THE 453 NARRATIVES HAVE NO LABEL AT ALL -- the field is present and empty in the source data, and the page's own info panel opens with a blank <h3> for them. Without the fallback the guide skipped every one: it said "231 narratives here" over a tab drawing 453, and half the artifact was unreachable by voice because of a gap in the data rather than anything about the tab. The fallback is the narrative's PROBLEM, clipped: it is always present, it is what the node actually is, and it is the one string a user could plausibly say back ("open positive geometry"). Clipping can make two narratives share a handle; matchItems then names both and asks, which is the right failure. Fixing the underlying data is a job for the generator, not for the guide -- but the guide must not pretend the unnamed ones are not there.

camera._note:
AN ORBIT CAMERA IS THREE NUMBERS AND A POINT. theta swings round the vertical axis, phi raises and lowers the eye, radius is the viewing distance, and cameraTarget is what it looks at; updateCameraPosition is the page's own function that turns the four into a camera position. Every camera verb is a step on one of them, so the declaration is paths and step sizes rather than code -- the same rule the item spec follows.
The numbers are the PAGE's, not invented: the clamps mirror onWheel (15..120) and the drag handler's phi guard (0.1 .. PI*0.85), so voice can never put the camera somewhere the mouse cannot. The orbit step is 0.4 rad, about what an 80-pixel drag does at the page's own 0.005 rad/px; the pan step is a quarter of the current viewing distance, so it feels the same close in and far out, exactly as the graph's pan scales with zoom.
PAN USES THE CAMERA'S OWN RIGHT AND UP, read off its world matrix. Panning along world axes would send the view sideways in a direction unrelated to what the user is looking at -- which after any rotation is nearly always.
